COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables design, estimated on a metropolitan-area panel (or repeated cross-sections if only limited time-series variation is available).

Why IV?  
• District fragmentation/choice is highly endogenous (politics, demographics, local tastes).  
• We possess an exogenous source of variation—natural geographic boundaries (rivers, large streams, lakes, coastal indentations, major ridge lines) that mechanically create potential “natural catchment areas” for school districts and hence drive the number of districts regardless of current educational or economic conditions.  
• These geographic features were fixed long before modern schooling, satisfy the relevance criterion, and are plausibly orthogonal to unobserved determinants of contemporary school productivity, private-school demand, and household sorting once we condition on broad metropolitan controls.  

Design outline  
First-stage: Fragmentation_msa = α + π·GeoFragment_msa + X′β + ε  
Second-stage: Y_msa = α₂ + γ·Fragmentation̂ _msa + X′β₂ + υ  

Y  ∈ {public-school productivity, private-school share, segregation indices, etc.}.  

If panel data are available, add metropolitan-area fixed effects and year fixed effects; the instrument is interacted with year dummies (“shift-share” style) or uses time-invariant geography whose impact is identified off consolidations/boundary changes over time.

================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
• Inter-district choice / fragmentation (e.g., number of districts per 10,000 public-school students; Herfindahl index of enrollment shares; inverse HHI). Higher value = more choice.

Control group  
• Metropolitan areas with low fragmentation (“monopoly” districts) serve as the counterfactual after instrumenting.

Treatment timing  
• Not a DID—fragmentation is quasi-time-invariant. If panel, changes stem from consolidations; otherwise cross-sectional IV.

Instrument (Z)  
• GeoFragment_msa = log(1 + length of rivers & major streams crossing potential school-boundary polygons divided by metro land area)  
Alternative/stronger set: number of unique land segments separated by water bodies; percent of land cut off by water; terrain-ruggedness index.

No running variable/cutoff (not an RDD).

================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance: Natural boundaries create exogenous costs of governing large, contiguous school districts, thereby increasing the equilibrium number of districts. (Testable: first-stage F > 10.)

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on controls, geographic boundaries affect today’s school outcomes only through their impact on district fragmentation, not by any other causal channel.

Plausibility: Rivers were drawn before 1900; we control for metro-level housing prices, land area, population density, transport costs, and historical manufacturing base to soak up any alternative mechanisms (e.g., rivers spurring commerce or urban form).

A3. Monotonicity: More natural boundaries never decrease fragmentation for any metro that would otherwise have consolidated—reasonable because boundaries cannot be “negative barriers.”

A4. Stable Unit (SUTVA): Outcomes in one metro area are unaffected by fragmentation in another; plausible at the MSA level.

================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Geography directly affects housing prices, commuting costs, or racial sorting, violating exclusion.  
Mitigation:  
• Control flexibly for topography (elevation s.d.), water-area share, coastal dummy, historical port dummy.  
• Placebo IV regressions on outcomes that should not respond to district fragmentation (e.g., contemporaneous homicide rates, median age) – find null effects.

Threat 2: Weak instrument in flat/arid metros (few rivers).  
Mitigation:  
• Report first-stage F-statistic.  
• Augment instrument set with additional exogenous geographic shifters (coastline length, number of islands, terrain ruggedness).  
• Use Limited-Information Maximum-Likelihood (LIML) and Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals as robustness.

Threat 3: Selection of metropolitan boundaries (MSA definitions) might correlate with fragmentation and outcomes.  
Mitigation:  
• Re-estimate using alternative spatial aggregations: Core-Based Statistical Areas, commuting zones.  
• Include historical population (1900, 1950) and state fixed effects.  
• Cluster standard errors at the state level.

================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# --- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS / IV with clustering
library(modelsummary)

# --- 1. Load data ----
metro <- read_csv("metro_level_school_data.csv")   # one row per MSA-year

# --- 2. Variable construction ----
metro <- metro %>% 
  mutate(
    fragmentation = n_districts / (public_enroll / 10000),       # districts per 10k students
    geo_fragment  = log1p(river_length_km / land_area_km2),      # instrument
    prod          = test_score_index / (spending_per_pupil),     # productivity
    year_factor   = as.factor(year)
  )

# --- 3. Baseline IV regression ----
iv_prod <- feols(prod ~ 1 | 
                 fragmentation ~ geo_fragment + year_factor + 
                 pop_log + land_area_km2 + median_income + pct_black + state_factor,
                 data = metro, cluster = "state_factor")

iv_private <- feols(private_school_share ~ 1 | 
                    fragmentation ~ geo_fragment + year_factor + 
                    pop_log + land_area_km2 + median_income + pct_black + state_factor,
                    data = metro, cluster = "state_factor")

# --- 4. Results table ----
modelsummary(list(iv_prod, iv_private),
             gof_omit = "Adj|Within|Pseudo")

# --- 5. Robustness: alternative instrument + placebo outcome ----
metro <- metro %>% mutate(
    terrain_inst = log1p(terrain_ruggedness)
)

iv_alt <- feols(prod ~ 1 | 
                fragmentation ~ geo_fragment + terrain_inst + year_factor + 
                controls + state_factor,
                data = metro, cluster = "state_factor")

# Placebo: violent crime rate (should be zero)
iv_placebo <- feols(violent_crime_rate ~ 1 | 
                    fragmentation ~ geo_fragment + year_factor + controls + state_factor,
                    data = metro, cluster = "state_factor")
```

================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory of Tiebout competition predicts that more inter-district choice pressures districts to produce higher achievement per tax dollar and reduces the need for private schooling; it may, however, increase racial and income sorting because mobile households self-select.

Prior signs:  
• γ_productivity > 0 : 1 sd increase in fragmentation raises productivity by ~0.10 sd.  
• γ_private_share < 0 : 1 sd increase lowers private-school share by 2–3 p.p.  
• γ_segregation > 0 : higher White/Black dissimilarity index by ~0.05.

Magnitudes are conjectural and guided by earlier work on school competition.

================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) – 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible given controls/placebos – 0.5  
C3: Monotonicity (no “defiers”) – 1  
C4: SUTVA / no cross-metro spillovers – 1  
C5: Correct functional form & robust standard errors – 0.5  

Total score: 4 / 5.
